content: Natural oil polyols (NOPs) are specialized polyols derived from vegetable oils through various chemical processes. These compounds are primarily utilized in the production of polyurethanes. According to the Farm Security and Rural Investment Act of 2002, most NOPs qualify as biobased products. While NOPs share common sources and applications, their chemical properties can vary significantly depending on the production method. They are typically clear liquids, ranging in color from colorless to medium yellow, with viscosities that depend on molecular weight and the number of hydroxyl groups per molecule. Higher molecular weights and hydroxyl content result in increased viscosity. A notable characteristic of NOPs is their odor, which varies between different types of NOPs. This odor is often a result of the chemical similarity of NOPs to their parent vegetable oils, making them susceptible to rancidity. Rancidity occurs due to the autoxidation of fatty acid chains containing carbon-carbon double bonds, leading to the formation of low molecular weight aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, which are responsible for the unpleasant odor. This odor is undesirable not only in the NOPs themselves but also in the polyurethane products made from them. Only a limited number of vegetable oils naturally contain unreacted hydroxyl groups, which are essential for the reactivity of NOPs. Castor oil is the only commercially available natural oil polyol that is directly derived from a plant source without requiring chemical modification. Other NOPs are produced by chemically modifying vegetable oils. The use of renewable resources like vegetable oils as feedstocks for chemical processes is intended to reduce reliance on non-renewable fossil fuels and decrease greenhouse gas emissions, particularly carbon dioxide. Studies estimate that the production of NOPs results in 36% lower global warming emissions, a 61% reduction in non-renewable energy use, and a 23% decrease in total energy demand compared to polyols derived from petrochemicals. Sources of Natural Oil Polyols Castor oil is primarily composed of ricinoleic acid, which constitutes 90% of its fatty acid content. Ricinoleic acid contains a hydroxyl group on the 12th carbon and a carbon-carbon double bond. The major component of castor oil is a tri-ester formed from ricinoleic acid and glycerin. Other vegetable oils, such as soybean oil, peanut oil, and canola oil, contain carbon-carbon double bonds but lack hydroxyl groups. To introduce hydroxyl groups into these oils, several chemical processes are employed, most of which involve oxidation of the carbon-carbon double bonds. One method involves treating vegetable oils with ozone, which cleaves the double bonds. Depending on the processing conditions, the resulting ozonolysis products can be converted into esters or alcohols. For example, the reaction of triolein with ozone and ethylene glycol produces hydroxyl-containing compounds. Another method, air oxidation (autoxidation), involves radical reactions that increase molecular weight and introduce hydroxyl groups. This process is also responsible for the drying of drying oils and can produce a complex mixture of crosslinked and oxidized triglycerides. Vegetable oils can also be treated with peroxy acids to form epoxides, which can then react with nucleophiles to generate hydroxyl groups. This process can be performed in a single step. Additionally, unsaturated fatty acids or their methyl esters can undergo hydroformylation, where carbon monoxide and hydrogen are used in the presence of a metal catalyst to add formyl (-CHO) groups to the carbon chain. Subsequent hydrogenation converts these formyl groups into hydroxyl groups. If the starting material is a methyl ester (similar to biodiesel), further reactions like transesterification may be required to produce polyols. Uses of Natural Oil Polyols Castor oil has a wide range of applications, many of which are attributed to the presence of its hydroxyl group. This functional group allows for chemical modifications that enhance the properties of castor oil compared to other vegetable oils lacking hydroxyl groups. Castor oil can undergo most reactions typical of alcohols, but its most significant industrial application is its reaction with diisocyanates to produce polyurethanes. Castor oil has been used to manufacture various polyurethane products, including coatings and foams. For instance, castor oil derivatized with propylene oxide is used to produce polyurethane foam for mattresses, while other derivatives are employed in coatings. Beyond castor oil, which is relatively expensive and not widely produced in many industrialized countries, the use of polyols derived from other vegetable oils for polyurethane production has gained attention since around 2004. This interest is driven by rising petrochemical feedstock costs and increasing consumer demand for environmentally friendly products. One prominent advocate for polyurethanes made from NOPs is the Ford Motor Company, which announced plans to use polyurethane foam made from NOPs in the seats of its 2008 Ford Mustang. Automakers have shown significant interest in NOP-based polyurethane products for use in car seats, headrests, armrests, soundproofing, and even body panels. NOPs are also used in polyurethane slab foam for conventional and memory foam mattresses. One of the earliest applications of NOPs, aside from castor oil, was in the production of spray-on polyurethane foam insulation for buildings.
